_description: Single source of truth for the app: the case-level session schema (forum/jurisdiction lives here, asked once) plus the index of every issue file in content/issues/.

forum.prompt: Is this motion being filed in state or federal court?
forum.asked: once, at the very start of the wizard, before any issue-taxonomy questions — every issue's law_paragraph rendering reads this instead of asking again
forum.note: SCOTUS authority binds state courts too, so a state-court filing always includes SCOTUS + the selected state together — there is no 'state only, no SCOTUS' option.

state_name.asked: once, only if forum is 'State court'
state_name.note: Currently only one option, matching this project's present scope. Its value maps to the court code 'AK' used throughout rule_statements' authorities. Expanding to a new state later means adding a dropdown option here and a new court value (e.g. 'CA') on the affected authorities — no other structural change.

federal_circuit.asked: once, only if forum is 'Federal court'
federal_circuit.note: Currently only one option, matching this project's present scope. Its value is used directly as the court code. Expanding to a new circuit later means adding a dropdown option here and using its name as a new court value.

case_session_schema.answers: object — keyed by question id, populated as the attorney moves through each issue's trigger.questions
case_session_schema.matched_issues: array of issue ids — populated by matching logic, not asked directly

circuits_reviewed_field.location: top level of each issue file, e.g. issue.circuits_reviewed
circuits_reviewed_field.format: array of court values (from federal_circuit) that have actually been checked for their OWN case law on this issue, e.g. ['9th Circuit'] — a circuit CAN be in this list with no circuit-specific authority added to any rule statement yet, meaning 'checked, nothing beyond SCOTUS worth citing'
circuits_reviewed_field.why_separate_from_rule_statements: Without this, there's no way to distinguish 'checked, nothing circuit-specific to add' from 'nobody has looked yet' — both look identical (no circuit-specific authority anywhere in the issue) unless tracked explicitly.
circuits_reviewed_field.tracked_at_issue_level_only: Deliberately NOT tracked per rule statement, even though citations now resolve per statement (see rule_statements_schema) — that would be more precise but more bookkeeping than needed. One issue-level field is enough.
circuits_reviewed_field.current_scope: Only ever contains '9th Circuit' for now, since that's the only circuit in scope.

review_condition_rendering.description: Separate from resolveLawParagraph. After an issue is matched (or considered) and its law_paragraph text is rendered, check the issue's review_conditions: for each one whose 'when' evaluates true against case_session.answers, append its display_note to the output.
review_condition_rendering.format: Append on its own line after the law paragraph text, wrapped as: [NOTE: <display_note>] — all-caps 'NOTE' and brackets so it's visually distinct from the drafted law text when the attorney reviews the output.
review_condition_rendering.why_separate_from_flag: 'flag' is a short machine-readable id (for logging/analytics — e.g. tracking how often intent_below_franks_standard fires across cases). 'display_note' is the attorney-facing sentence that actually explains the judgment call. Never surface 'flag' itself in the output — it's not written for a human reader.

excluded_explanations_rendering.description: For issues whose match_condition did NOT pass, check excluded_explanations: if any entry's 'when' evaluates true against case_session.answers, the issue was a close call worth explaining, even though it isn't included in the motion.
steps: 1. For every issue considered (not just matched ones), if match_condition failed, check its excluded_explanations list.
2. Collect { issue_label, display_note } for each entry whose 'when' evaluates true.

3. If any were collected, render them together in ONE section at the very end of the full document — after all matched issues' law paragraphs/notes, and after cross_cutting_reminders — e.g. under a heading like 'Issues Considered But Not Included'.
4. If nothing was collected, omit the section entirely — don't show an empty heading.
excluded_explanations_rendering.why_separate_from_review_conditions: review_conditions flags a shaky INCLUDED issue, rendered inline with that issue's law paragraph. excluded_explanations explains a NOT-included issue, rendered once at the end since there's no law paragraph to attach it to — the issue never made it into the motion body at all.
excluded_explanations_rendering.why_not_every_failed_match_gets_one: Most excluded issues fail match_condition simply because the fact pattern doesn't exist for this case (e.g. no warrant was used at all) — that's not a close call and needs no explanation. excluded_explanations only fires for the specific, legally meaningful near-misses you've deliberately documented, not every unmatched issue.

cross_cutting_reminders.description: Standing and fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree/attenuation aren't triggered by a specific fact pattern the way most issues are — they apply to EVERY suppression issue, always. Rather than referencing them per-issue (which doesn't scale and is easy to forget on any given issue file), render a single reminder once per motion, whenever at least one issue matched — not once per matched issue.

reminders.display_note: Before relying on any issue above, confirm the defendant has standing to challenge it — i.e., a reasonable expectation of privacy in the place or thing searched. Standing is assessed separately for each matched issue; having it for one doesn't establish it for another.

For each matched issue, consider whether the evidence you're seeking to suppress is a direct or derivative product of that violation, versus sufficiently attenuated to survive suppression even if the underlying issue is found.

cross_cutting_reminders.rendering: Render once at the end of the motion's full output (after every matched issue's law paragraph and notes), not repeated per issue.

rule_statements_schema.description: law_paragraph is an ORDERED LIST of small rule statements (law_paragraph.rule_statements), not a fixed set of whole-paragraph segments per court. Each statement is one sentence, or two at most — one proposition — with its own authorities array. Rendering walks the list in order, and for each statement includes only the authorities whose court is actually desired for this motion — so the SAME statement can render with just a SCOTUS citation in a federal motion, a genuine SCOTUS + state PARALLEL citation in a state motion (e.g. 'Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015); Simmons v. State, 435 P.3d 975 (Alaska App. 2018)'), or a lone state/circuit citation if that's genuinely all that exists for that specific point.

shape.id: short slug, unique within the issue
shape.text: a BARE proposition. NEVER embed a case name or citation in this text, even mid-sentence — e.g. 'Illinois v. Caballes permits a dog sniff...' is wrong; write 'A dog sniff is permissible only if...' instead, and put Caballes in authorities. This can be a direct quotation — the whole quotation is then the proposition.
shape.authorities: see authority_schema — every entry here is understood to support exactly this statement's text, nothing more, nothing less

rule_statements_schema.why_this_replaced_segments: The earlier model had one whole paragraph per court (a 'federal_rule' segment, a 'state_rule' segment), concatenated when both applied. That could only ever produce two separate paragraphs saying the same thing twice — it structurally could not produce a genuine parallel citation within one sentence. Breaking the paragraph into atomic, independently-citable statements lets each proposition resolve its own citation(s) independently.
rule_statements_schema.omission_behavior: If a statement's authorities produce no match for the desired courts (e.g. only a state citation exists, but the motion is federal-only), the ENTIRE statement — sentence and all — is omitted from the rendered paragraph. Never show a bare, uncited sentence.
rule_statements_schema.research_completeness_tracked_at_issue_l: A statement lacking an AK authority does NOT mean 'confirmed nothing exists' — it just isn't attached yet. Whether a given court has actually been researched for an issue is tracked by circuits_reviewed / jurisdiction_status at the ISSUE level (unchanged), not per statement — a deliberate choice to avoid unnecessary bookkeeping granularity.
rule_statements_schema.no_more_placeholder_objects: There is no more NEEDS_RESEARCH segment-level placeholder, and no more empty-string placeholder text sitting in a file. A statement you haven't finished researching for a given court simply has no authority entry for that court — nothing to blank out, nothing that could be mistaken for real content at a skim.

authority_schema.description: Every legal authority cited anywhere lives inside a rule statement's 'authorities' array (see rule_statements_schema). Each entry carries a 'type' (case/statute/constitution/rule) and a 'court' field.

shape.name: the case name, or the statute/rule/constitutional provision identifier
shape.citation: reporter citation for a case; empty string for statute/constitution/rule, where 'name' already IS the citation

authority_schema.why_no_propositions_field: A rule statement is deliberately atomic — one sentence, one proposition. Every authority attached to it necessarily supports that same single point, so a separate 'propositions' field on each authority would just re-paraphrase the statement's own text, which is already more complete and more accurate than any shorthand summary. If a statement seems to need two different propositions tracked separately across its authorities, that's a sign it should be split into two rule statements instead.
authority_schema.why_court_not_jurisdiction: A separate 'jurisdiction' field (federal/state) plus a 'circuit'/'state' field was the same redundancy problem fixed once already at the segment level (segments have since been eliminated entirely — see rule_statements_schema). One 'court' value says everything needed, more precisely.
authority_schema.migration_history: citations (case-shaped, per-segment) -> statutory_citations stopgap -> unified 'authorities' array with a 'jurisdiction' field, per-segment -> 'court' field replacing 'jurisdiction', still per-segment -> segments eliminated entirely; 'authorities' now lives on each atomic rule statement instead, with 'propositions' dropped since the statement's own text already is the proposition.

court_tagging_convention.SCOTUS: court: 'SCOTUS' on an authority — genuine U.S. Supreme Court authority only, including the U.S. Constitution as SCOTUS interprets it. Binding on federal and state courts alike, so an authority tagged this way is included in EVERY rendering of the rule statement it's attached to, regardless of forum. Do NOT tag a circuit-level case 'SCOTUS' just because you haven't found a split — if it isn't actually a Supreme Court case, tag it with the real circuit instead.
court_tagging_convention.circuit_specific: court: '9th Circuit' — included in a statement's rendering only when case_session.federal_circuit matches (i.e. only in a 'Federal court' filing in that circuit). Add one whenever the 9th Circuit has its own case on a statement's proposition — routine, not limited to genuine splits. NEVER included in a 'State court' rendering, even on the same statement — the 9th Circuit isn't binding on Alaska's state courts.
court_tagging_convention.state_specific: court: 'AK' — included only when case_session.state_name matches (i.e. only in a 'State court' filing). Also used for AK statutes, constitutional provisions, and court rules — 'court' means 'whose law this authority represents', not literally 'which court decided it'.
court_tagging_convention.current_scope: Only three court values are in use right now — SCOTUS, 9th Circuit, and AK — matching the one-option dropdowns in case_session_schema. Expanding later just means a new dropdown option plus tagging new authorities with the new court value — no change to rule_statements structure or the resolver.
court_tagging_convention.history: This value space was previously attached to whole SEGMENTS (one court per paragraph-sized chunk). Segments were eliminated in favor of per-statement 'authorities' arrays (see rule_statements_schema) once it became clear a genuine parallel citation requires resolving citations within one sentence, not choosing between whole alternate paragraphs. The court values and their meaning carried over unchanged — only the level they attach to moved from segment to individual authority.

applicable_courts_field.location: top level of each issue file, e.g. issue.applicable_courts
applicable_courts_field.format: array of court values (same value space as authority.court — 'SCOTUS' | '9th Circuit' | 'AK') — which courts this ISSUE is known to exist in at all, regardless of research status.
applicable_courts_field.why_court_not_forum: An earlier version used 'applicable_forums': ['State court'] — but 'state court' wrongly implies the issue applies in ANY state. The three chemical-test-rights issues are known to exist only under Alaska's specific implied-consent statute; whether an equivalent exists elsewhere hasn't been checked and must not be assumed. 'applicable_courts': ['AK'] says exactly what's known.
applicable_courts_field.scotus_alone_is_universal: Listing 'SCOTUS' alone is sufficient to mean 'applies in every circuit and every state' — desiredCourts always includes SCOTUS regardless of forum, so the intersection is guaranteed non-empty. Do NOT also list '9th Circuit' and 'AK' alongside SCOTUS for a genuinely federal-constitutional issue — that's redundant, not extra-safe. Only list a specific court ALONE (no SCOTUS) when the issue is NOT grounded in SCOTUS doctrine and is known to exist only in that court's own law.
applicable_courts_field.how_it_differs_from_content_coverage: This is about whether an issue exists in a court at all, not whether content has been written for it yet. Whether an authority has actually been added for a given circuit/state on any rule statement (and circuits_reviewed) is a completely separate, finer-grained question from this field.
how_it_is_checked: Decision tree / wizard: compute desiredCourts from case_session (see resolver_logic). Before asking an issue's trigger questions at all, skip the entire issue if desiredCourts has no overlap with issue.applicable_courts.
resolveLawParagraph (see resolver_logic step 1): same intersection check. An issue with no overlap is skipped entirely — no warning, no fallback, nothing rendered.
applicable_courts_field.current_values: ['SCOTUS'] for all three Fourth Amendment issues (franks-violation, prolonged-stop, passenger-frisk-suspicionless). ['AK'] only for all three chemical-test-rights issues.

steps: 0. desiredCourts = forumToCourts(case_session) — 'State court' -> {SCOTUS, courtCodeForState(case_session.state_name)} e.g. {SCOTUS, AK}; 'Federal court' -> {SCOTUS, case_session.federal_circuit} e.g. {SCOTUS, 9th Circuit}
1. IF desiredCourts has NO overlap with issue.applicable_courts: skip this issue entirely — no warning, no output. See applicable_courts_field.

2. FOR each statement in issue.law_paragraph.rule_statements, in order: (a) matchingAuthorities = statement.authorities where authority.court IN desiredCourts; (b) IF matchingAuthorities is empty, omit this statement entirely from the rendered paragraph; (c) ELSE render as statement.text + ' ' + citationString(matchingAuthorities) + '.' — see citation_string_formatting.
3. text = the rendered (non-omitted) statements from step 2, concatenated in order with a space between them
4. authorities = every matchingAuthorities collected across all rendered statements, flattened

5. IF every statement was omitted in step 2 (text is empty): set warning 'no_authority_found' — shouldn't normally happen for an applicable issue, since the core SCOTUS-backed statement(s) should always match, but worth catching explicitly rather than silently returning nothing

6. IF case_session.forum == 'Federal court' AND case_session.federal_circuit NOT IN issue.circuits_reviewed: add soft warning 'circuit_specific_authority_not_researched' — fires even when text is non-empty, since it means nobody has checked whether this circuit has its own authority worth adding to any rule statement yet. NEVER fires for a 'State court' filing.
7. return { text, authorities, warnings: [] }  // warnings is a list — both a step-5 and step-6 warning can fire together

citation_string_formatting.description: How resolver_logic step 2c turns a statement's matchingAuthorities into the trailing citation text.
citation_string_formatting.single_authority: IF authority.citation is non-empty (a case): '<name>, <citation>' — e.g. 'Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015)'. IF authority.citation is empty (statute/rule/constitution, where name already IS the citation): just '<name>' — e.g. 'AS 28.35.033(e)'.
citation_string_formatting.multiple_authorities: Join with '; ' (semicolon-space) — this is what produces a genuine parallel citation, e.g. 'Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015); Simmons v. State, 435 P.3d 975 (Alaska App. 2018)'.
citation_string_formatting.ordering: SCOTUS first, then circuit, then state — matches the SCOTUS-first convention used elsewhere in this project.

question_types.multiple_choice: answer is a single string, one of the question's options — pick exactly one
question_types.multi_select: answer is an array of strings, a subset of the question's options — pick any number, including zero or all
question_types.short_text: answer is a free-text string, not matched against a fixed option list — used for fact-gathering (e.g. q_duration), not for gating match_condition

condition_shape.description: The shape used by match_condition, and by 'when' inside review_conditions/excluded_explanations, is the same: either a single leaf { question, op, value } or a compound { all: [...] } / { any: [...] } of leaves (and compounds can nest).

ops_for_scalar_answers.description: For yes_no and multiple_choice questions (answer is a single string).

ops_for_array_answers.description: For multi_select questions (answer is an array of strings). Do NOT use equals/in against a multi_select answer — those compare a single value and give unreliable results against an array.

ops.includes: true if the given value (a single option string) is present anywhere in the answer array
ops.not_includes: true if the given value is absent from the answer array
ops.not_empty: true if at least one option was selected, regardless of which — value is omitted for this op
ops.empty: true if no options were selected — value is omitted for this op

coverage_note: To check how much research remains, scan all issue files' rule_statements for authorities missing a given court, or check jurisdiction_status/circuits_reviewed across the issues array.
